attributes.title: Level 3

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use comments to create multiple sections in the editor to better organize your code?
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by adding code comments to organize where the code will go in the editor!


Add comments with these descriptions to the project: set up, sprite code, A button pressed, A button released.


Start each comment with // and create several blank lines between each comment.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you type a number between 1-15 to set the color parameter in the parentheses in scene.setBackgroundColor(color)?
steps.instructions:
Set up the project with a background color and a dialog box with instructions.


Open Scene, drag [set background color to (color)] under //set up. Set a color parameter using a number between 1-15.


Open Game and drag [set dialog frame to (frame)] under //set up underneath the background color code. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:


game.setDialogFrame(img` `)

Click the palette to the left of the line of code to choose a dialog frame image from the Gallery. Scroll down in the Gallery to access the dialog frame options.


Then, open Game and drag [show long text (str) (layout)] underneath the code to set the dialog frame. The showLongText function takes two parameters: string and layout. In the parentheses, replace the first argument, null with a string in quotation marks that tells the user to press the A button to play the game. Then, update the second argument by highlighting .Bottom and retyping . and selecting a new screen position from the code completion tool. 


Click ▶ to see the background color and dialog box appear on screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add a score counter to the project?
steps.instructions:
Add a score counter to keep track of the number of button presses!


Open Info, drag out [set score to (value)] under // set up underneath the dialog box code. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

info.setScore(0)

The setScore function takes one parameter: value. Use the default argument of 0 to set the score to 0 when the project starts.


Click ▶ to see the score counter appear on screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add a sprite, select its image, and update its name?
steps.instructions:
Add the A button sprite to the project!


Open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] underneath // sprite code. Click the palette to select the A button sprite. Then, replace mySprite by typing a simple name using camelCase that describes what it is, such as buttonSprite.


Then, set the sprite’s position by opening Sprites and dragging [set (mySprite) position to x y] underneath the code that sets the sprite. Replace mySprite with the sprite’s name. Update the x (0-160)  and y (0-120) parameters so that the sprite appears near the middle of the screen.


Click ▶ to see the sprite appear on screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add controller.Button event code under // A button pressed and // A button released, and update the event argument to match the comments?
steps.instructions:
Control what happens when the A button is pressed, and when it is released.


Open Controller and drag out [run code on (button) button (event)] underneath both the // A button pressed and // A button released comments. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:


controller.A.onEvent
(ControllerButtonEvent.Pressed, 
function( ) {...} )

In JavaScript, curly brackets { } are used to create block statements, or indented lines of code that will run inside of another line of code, such as an event or loop. The curly brackets create a “container” for the block statement, like the containers used in the blocks editor.


The controller.Button event has 1 property: Button, and takes 2 parameters: event and handler. In the code under // A button pressed, use the default property A and default event argument ControllerButtonEvent.Pressed.


In the code under // A button released, use the default property A but delete .Pressed then retype the dot operator . to select Released from the code completion tool.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the sprite to appear as a different image when the A button is pressed and released?
steps.instructions:
Change the button image when the A button is pressed, and again when it is released.


Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) image to (img)] inside the curly brackets { } of both controller.A events. Notice how the code is indented and turns into JavaScript text: 

mySprite.setImage(img)

Replace mySprite with the sprite’s name for both lines of code. Click the palette to the left of the line of code to choose the “pressed” button image in the first block statement, and the “released” button image in the other block statement.


Click ▶ to see the button sprite’s image change as the A button is pressed.

steps.hints:
❓ Did you code the changeScoreBy function inside the curly brackets { } of the controller.A.onEvent

(ControllerButtonEvent.Pressed) event?
steps.instructions:
Change the score every time the A button is pressed.


Open Info and drag [change score by (1)] inside the curly brackets { } of the controller.A.onEvent

(ControllerButtonEvent.Pressed) event. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

info.changeScoreBy(1)

The changeScoreBy function takes 1 parameter: value, or the number that the score will change by. Use the default argument 1 or change it to a different number to adjust the number of points the score changes by, each time the A button is pressed.


Click ▶ to see the score increase each time the A button is pressed.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you switch back to the blocks editor? What looks similar and what looks different?
steps.instructions:
Test out the project. Does it work as expected?


Switch to the blocks editor to see what the JavaScript code looks like in blocks! Notice what is similar about the code, and what looks different: how do the block statements inside the curly brackets appear in blocks, versus in JavaScript?

subgroups.title: Button Clicker!
subgroups.introduction: Create a clicker game project in JavaScript that uses block statements with events that control the A button!

validationItems.text: Use the setScore function to set the score to 0.
Use 1 sprite with a custom name and set its position.
Use the on button pressed event.
Use the on button released event.
Use 2 set image functions to change the button’s appearance.
Use the change score function to update the score every time a button is pressed.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 3 of Blue Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about block statements. In JavaScript, instead of adding code into different containers, you’ll add block statements inside curly brackets { } of an event or a loop. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 3:

badges.title: Thinking Inside the Block
badges.description: Use block statements inside curly brackets { } to add code inside of events and loops.

badges.title: Projectile Manager
badges.description: Create a  projectile in JavaScript.

badges.title: Game On (Update Interval)
badges.description: Use a game update loop in JavaScript.

badges.title: About Yay High
badges.description: Use the screen object’s height property instead of a number.

badges.title: Framing the Discussion
badges.description: Use setDialogFrame to design a custom text box.

badges.title: Settle the Score
badges.description: Set the score in JavaScript.

badges.title: Cute as a Button
badges.description: Use a button event in JavaScript.
